title: Tulkus
hook: teachers recognized as rebirths of earlier masters

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kalachakra, the wheel of time, and a sand mandala swept away. Your line was the wheel of time. When you checked the clock, did that one place come to mind? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

A few visitors arrive at a farmhouse, dressed plainly. On a table they set down some objects: two rosaries, two walking sticks, two small drums. One of each pair belonged to a teacher who died some years before. The other is a look-alike. A small child toddles over, studies them, and reaches, without much fuss, for the ones that were the teacher's. The visitors glance at each other. This is the kind of scene told in the stories of how a tulku is found. It isn't the whole process, and it isn't proof on its own. But it is how a search can end.
screen: `OBJECTS SET IN PAIRS.` → `A CHILD REACHES FOR THE TEACHER'S.` → `THE SEARCH ENDS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Tulku is Tibetan, and it's the word used to translate the Sanskrit nirmanakaya, the emanation body: the form in which awakened mind appears in the world. In everyday Tibetan use, a tulku is a teacher recognized as the rebirth of an earlier master. Second, the idea underneath. In Buddhist teaching, beings are ordinarily carried into rebirth by their karma. A tulku is understood differently: a teacher who, out of compassion, chooses to return, to carry on the work with the same students and the same monastery. The Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas are both lines of this kind, each one recognized as the return of the one before. Third, the finding. Tradition describes several signs, and searchers weigh them together: a letter the teacher left about where to look, the dreams and visions of senior lamas, omens around a birth, and finally the child, tested with things that were the teacher's. Then a recognition is announced, and the child is taken to be raised and educated in the monastery. Fourth, the honest part. Tibetan teachers speak about this openly. Recognitions have sometimes been disputed, and politics has sometimes pressed in. And teachers are clear that a title is a beginning, not a finish line: a recognized tulku still has to study for years, take vows, practice, and earn the trust of students like anyone else. What the system holds onto is a thread. A teacher, a monastery, a community of students, and the hope that the one who cared for them has returned.
screen: `TULKU: THE EMANATION BODY.` · `ONE WHO CHOOSES TO RETURN.` · `LETTERS, DREAMS, A CHILD'S HAND.` · `A TITLE IS A BEGINNING.` · then, large: `RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a lineage. If you have something that came down to you from an older generation, a ring, a book, a tool, a recipe card, hold it in your hands. If not, rest your open hands on your knees and think of one thing you know how to do that came down that way. Settle, and breathe. Then let the line run backward: who had it before you, and before them, a chain of hands longer than you can see. You don't need names. Just let the line be there behind you, and let a quiet thank-you travel down the whole length of it. The bell holds the time.
Tulku. The emanation body: in Tibet, a teacher recognized as the return of an earlier master, who must still study and practice. Today's word.
Your line: returned. Today, do one thing the way someone who taught you would have done it, and let them come back for a moment through your hands. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, when certain teachers die, senior lamas search for their rebirth using letters, dreams, signs and tests with the teacher's belongings; a recognized child, called a tulku, is then raised and educated in the monastery.

fork.reveal: the test is one sign among several. a recognized child begins years of study: a title is a beginning, not a finish line.

original.note: Tibetan sprul sku: sprul, emanation, and sku, body. It renders the Sanskrit nirmanakaya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a reincarnated holy child.
what it means: a teacher recognized as the return of an earlier master, who still has to study and earn trust.
what a scholar hears: sprul sku, emanation body, rendering the Sanskrit nirmanakaya; recognized lines include the Karmapas and the Dalai Lamas.

notes: The hook's object test is told as a typical scene from the stories, not as a specific recognition; confirm it is fair.

'Recognitions have sometimes been disputed, and politics has sometimes pressed in' is kept general on purpose; no specific case (for example the Panchen Lama) is named. A Keeper may prefer more or less here.
The Karmapa line is often described as the earliest tulku line; that claim was left out under the claims rule.
Dalai Lamas as emanations of Avalokiteshvara is not mentioned; could be added.
